newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan cricket hero sets sights on power.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan cricket hero sets sights on power.

text.p: Former international cricket star Imran Khan launched a drive on Friday to become Pakistan's next prime minister, saying his fledgling movement would clean up rampant corruption and stand up to foreign interests.

"It is time for fresh faces to come into Pakistan's politics," Khan, surrounded by members of his Tehreek-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) party, told a news conference. "The people of Pakistan are fed up with the same faces and corrupt money."
Khan, 43, announced his candidacy as shock waves continued to rumble through Pakistan's political system after the dismissal of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto on Tuesday.
President Farooq Leghari ordered the dissolution of the provincial assembly of Baluchistan province on Friday, the second regional parliament to be disbanded in two days.
On Thursday he dismissed the assembly in the industrialised province of Sindh, where Bhutto has her ancestral home, and named an estranged uncle of Bhutto as caretaker chief minister.
Leghari summarily sacked Bhutto with a pre-dawn order on Tuesday, accusing her administration of corruption and misrule.
Political sources said assemblies in the two other provinces -- Punjab and North West Frontier -- could be dissolved soon.
Bhutto prepared on Friday to launch a two-pronged campaign to recapture power.

She said she expected to file a legal challenge next week to Leghari's order toppling her government. She vowed to tour the country to whip up support for her Pakistan People's Party (PPP), now that the four-day-old caretaker government had lifted curbs on her movements.
Although untested in politics, Khan was sure to complicate matters for the two dominant parties as they gear up for polls set for February 3, and his party could at least be a spoiler.

Photogenic and admired for leading Pakistan to victory in the 1992 World Cup, Khan is respected for his achievement in raising funds to build a cancer hospital in the provincial capital Lahore, and appeals largely to the urban middle class.
A playboy in youth, he later rediscovered his Islamic roots. Last year he raised some eyebrows by marrying Jemima Goldsmith, jet-setting daughter of Anglo-French financier James Goldsmith.
But critics say the party's still undefined programme, focusing on corruption and Islam, could seem austere to many.

Khan said his party, which had been reluctant to take part in the elections unless a full-blown anti-corruption drive was first completed, decided during an all-night meeting to contest the polls and try to put up candidates in all constituencies.

Khan said Tehreek-i-Insaaf, formed in April, demanded that any candidates in the elections declare their assets and taxes paid. He was surrounded by his newly appointed executive committee whose members are also largely new to politics.
Asked what his qualifications were, Khan, who once captained Pakistan's national cricket squad and conceded he had never voted, said: "I feel that I'm better qualified than the lot."
Khan was asked to describe his policies towards foreign governments and the International Monetary Fund, which is in talks with Pakistan over reviving a stalled $600 million loan.
"We should not be a shameless country where you have to bend down in front of people every time you need money. I as a Pakistani am deeply offended by this," he said.
Asked if he would refuse to seek IMF loans, he said: "Put it this way, if there was a question of seeking loans, I would be very desperate."
